summary: A BBN note that the link field in the IMP/Host leader was widened by four bits and renamed the message-id field, so hosts could identify individual messages more uniquely and get more throughput. All 12 bits are returned in RFNMs and similar replies. Hosts need not use the extra bits.

eli5.summary: The label on each message got a bit longer, so computers could tell their messages apart and send more at once.

questions: what is the imp message-id field
how many bits is the message-id in the imp host leader
is the message-id change backward compatible
subtitle: BBN widens the IMP/Host link field by four bits so messages can be told apart.

tldr.problem: The IMP message format constrains network users to low throughput if messages are uniquely identified only by the link number.
tldr.mechanism: The link field in the IMP/Host and Host/IMP leaders is extended to the right by four bits (bits 17 to 28 of the leader) and renamed the message-id field.
tldr.outcome: All 12 bits are returned in RFNMs and INCOMPLETE TRANSMISSIONs, and hosts are free to ignore the extra bits, so the change is backward compatible.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 533 as Unknown and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The note itself says it should be kept with BBN Report 1822 until that report is updated.

sections.title: The Throughput Problem
sections.content:
The IMP message format is specified in BBN Report 1822. The note observes that this format constrains network users to low throughputs if messages are to be uniquely identified through the link number.

BBN reports that it has already implemented a change in the IMP/Host protocol to ease this difficulty.
sections.eli5: If every message only had a small label, you had to wait before sending the next one. That made sending slow.

sections.title: The Message-ID Field
sections.content:
The link field in the IMP/Host and Host/IMP leaders is extended to the right by four bits, so it now uses bits 17 to 28 of the leader. Its name changes to the message-id field, and it is expected to be used to identify messages uniquely between the IMPs and the Hosts.

All 12 bits of the message-id are returned to the Host in RFNMs, INCOMPLETE TRANSMISSIONs and similar replies. No ordering is implied by the field.
sections.eli5: The name tag on each message got four more spaces. The tag comes back with the reply so you know which message it was about.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Use
sections.content:
The Host/Host protocol uses the old link field to identify connections, so the four new bits might well be used to identify messages on a given connection (that is, over a given link). Hosts have no obligation to identify their messages uniquely, and the IMP subnetwork does not care.

Because a receiving Host does not have to look at the extra four bits, the change is completely backward compatible, even when senders do use them. The note asks readers to keep it with their copy of BBN Report 1822 until that report is updated.
sections.eli5: Nobody has to use the new spaces. Old computers still work, and new ones can use them if they want.
